title: Singleton pattern
idea: The Singleton pattern makes a class create exactly one instance and gives everyone a global way to reach it, usually through a static method.
points: A Singleton hides its constructor and hands out one shared instance.
A holder class or an `enum` gives lazy, thread-safe creation with no explicit lock.
Double-checked locking is correct only when the instance field is `volatile`.
`Runtime.getRuntime()` is a JDK Singleton; prefer DI for your own services.

hero.title: Two threads race a lazy Singleton

steps.caption: Thread A calls `getInstance` first and sees the field is still `null`.
The scheduler switches to Thread B before A writes. B also sees `null`.
Thread A builds Registry #1, stores it in the static field and returns it.
Thread B builds Registry #2 and overwrites the field. Two instances now exist.
A's caller keeps using #1, so anything it registers is invisible to everyone else.
Fix (see the code tab): with a holder class the JVM initialises the field once, under its class-init lock.
Both threads now receive the same object, and no explicit lock appears in your code.

code.title: Three thread-safe styles
code.caption: Eight threads race on first use; each style still builds exactly one instance.

walk.text: Eight threads hit all three Singletons at once, then `join` makes the output deterministic.
Holder idiom: `Holder` loads on the first `getInstance` call, and class init runs once.
`volatile` stops another thread seeing a reference to a half-built object.
Check, lock, check again: only callers that arrive before the instance exists take the lock.
An `enum` constant is created once by the JVM, and reflection cannot make another.
The counters show one construction each; the JVM's rules, not this run, guarantee it.
The JDK's own Singleton: `getRuntime` always returns the same object.

code.title: Why to avoid it
code.caption: A global Singleton leaks state between callers; an injected interface does not.

walk.text: A classic eager Singleton holding mutable state: a set of enabled flags.
`PriceService` reaches the global directly. Its constructor hides the dependency.
Test 1 turns a flag on. Test 2 inherits it, so results depend on test order.
The fix asks for a `Flags` in the constructor and rejects `null`.
Each caller passes its own flags. No shared state, no order dependence.

pitfalls: A lazy null check without a lock can build two instances when first calls overlap.
Double-checked locking without `volatile` may hand another thread a half-built object.
Static `getInstance` calls hide dependencies, and tests leak state; inject an interface instead.

quiz.why: `a` and `b` reference the single enum constant, so all three calls bump one counter, and `==` compares the same reference.

takeaway: Need one instance? Let DI share it, rather than a static global.
